stances.claim: The 37 petitions against the ATA -- listed in the SC Advisory -- make it 'the most assailed law in memory under the 1987 Constitution,' but this 'numerical superiority' is not commendable: 'repetitive pleas will ironically delay the resolution of the case,' as CJ warned in his August 16 column.

CJ's August 16 suggestion that petitioners 'unite and request the Court's permission... to put together all their petitions into only one united pleading' and 'set aside their ego and [desire for] media soundbites' has been ignored -- forcing the Court itself to do this 'chore' via the Advisory listing essential issues and directing coordination.

The substantive challenge is enormous: six procedural issues, 15 substantive issues, and one 'gripping' Anti-Terrorism Council issue with eight sub-issues that 'requires mastery of the long and short of constitutional law' -- meaning the presenting lawyers must 'prepare well... think on their feet... and face minute scrutiny by the justices.'

Asymmetric representation: 37 petitioner sets with multiple lawyers each vs. SolGen Calida (with up to 3 assistant lawyers), with super lawyer Estelito P. Mendoza's potential amicus participation still pending -- making the petitioners' coordination problem doubly costly.

Oral Arguments will not finish in one day; CJ's 'fervent hope' is that 'by their readiness and expertise, the presenting lawyers would illumine, edify, and assist the Court in promulgating a just and speedy decision.'

notable_anecdotes: The SC's own correction of the petitioners' coordination failure -- directing in the Advisory that counsels 'coordinate with each other and, thereafter, submit to the Court a manifestation stating: (a) the name/s of the presenting lawyer/s on each issue or group of issues; and (b) the time allotted for each lawyer, the total of which should not, however, exceed the time limit [of 30 minutes]' -- modeling the institutional cost of uncoordinated litigation.

Solicitor General Calida 'allowed [by the advisory] to bring with him during the Oral Arguments not more than three (3) lawyers' -- preserved as the asymmetry datum (one government voice; 37 petitioner sets).
Estelito P. Mendoza filed an amicus 'Comment' favoring respondents; Court has not yet acted -- modeling the layered-participation ecosystem of constitutional-challenge oral arguments.

ERRATA at the foot of the column -- correcting the Nov 22 column's Bongbong arithmetic paragraph and a Negros Occidental/Oriental error -- paired with the gentle institutional self-defense: 'However, the errors did not change the meaning, substance, or context of the column.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports on the Supreme Court's Advisory setting Oral Arguments for January 19, 2021 at 2 PM on the petitions challenging the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA), and observes that the 37 petitions listed by case number make the ATA 'the most assailed law in memory under the 1987 Constitution.' He flags the asymmetric stakes: 37 petitioner sets each with multiple lawyers vs. Solicitor General Jose C. Calida (allowed up to three assistant lawyers), with super lawyer Estelito P. Mendoza's amicus 'Comment' favoring the respondents still pending Court action. CJ recalls his August 16 column warning that 'repetitive pleas will ironically delay the resolution of the case' -- a prediction now vindicated, as the Court had to move its initially-aspired September Oral Arguments by four months because 'new petitions kept coming in, many of them echoing substantially the same issues and prayers.' His earlier suggestion that petitioners 'unite and request the Court's permission... to put together all their petitions into only one united pleading' and 'set aside their ego and [desire for] media soundbites' was ignored -- leaving the Court itself to do this 'chore' via the Advisory listing 'essential issues' and directing counsels to coordinate and submit manifestations naming presenting lawyers and time allotments (not exceeding 30 minutes). The substantive scope is daunting: six procedural issues, 15 substantive issues, plus one 'gripping' issue (with eight sub-issues) on the alleged 'excessive and arbitrary powers given to the Anti-Terrorism Council' that 'requires mastery of the long and short of constitutional law.' CJ does not expect Oral Arguments to finish in one day and closes with the aspirational hope that 'by their readiness and expertise, the presenting lawyers would illumine, edify, and assist the Court in promulgating a just and speedy decision.' An ERRATA at the foot corrects the November 22 column's Bongbong arithmetic paragraph and a Negros Occidental/Oriental slip, paired with the institutional self-defense that 'the errors did not change the meaning, substance, or context of the column.'
